newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia fears frost could harm sugarbeet further.
newsitem.headline: Serbia fears frost could harm sugarbeet further.

text.p: Serbia's sugar producers fear more frost could affect sugar beets already re-sown on some 10,000 hectares, an industry source said Monday.

"More frost could be a real disaster for the crop. Low temperatures in the past weeks have already destroyed newly-emerging beet plants on more than 10,000 ha," Milan Patkovic, of the sugar producer's association Jugosecer told Reuters.
"The soil temperature of between 1-2 degrees Celsius and snow does not worry us. Our fear is frost," he said.
Patkovic said re-sowing would increase production costs and late sowing would affect yields too.
"But we will continue the campaign till the end of the month instead of ending it around April 20 as planned," he said.
The situation on some 60,000 ha already sown is not known.
"We need at least two days of dry weather to get a real picture of plantings," Patkovic said. "
"But more reliable information will not be available until mid-May," he added.

This year's government beet area target was 100,000 ha, which figure was set to take up the capacity of the country's 15 refineries. The beet area in 1996 was some 70,000 ha yielding 2.391 million tonnes of sugarbeet.

According to the agriculture ministry, Serbia has 400,000-500,000 tonnes of white sugar in its reserves, more than enough to bridge the gap till the next harvest. Annual needs are estimated at 300,000 tonnes.

Experts say the figure, announced by the agriculture minister last week, was realistic considering large white and raw sugar 1996 imports, domestic production of 270,000 tonnes and 50,000 tonnes of sugar in stock from 1995.

But some analysts disagreed with the minister's forecast that the price of sugar could fall to under two dinars per kilo from 2.90-3.00 dinars, well below the state's set price of 4.86 dinars per kilo.

"The price of sugar could remain stable at around three dinars per kilo for a while. But frost and bad weather will inevitably push the sugar price up," said industry expert who asked not to be named. --Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom ++381 11 222 4254
